Definite integrals

The definite integral ∫abf(x) dx adds up f(x) over the interval from a to b: geometrically, it is the signed area between the graph and the x-axis. This calculator uses two clearly labelled methods: an exact answer from the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus whenever it can find an antiderivative, and a numerical answer from adaptive Simpson's rule otherwise. The exact answer is always cross-checked numerically.

Try changing the input

Integrate sin⁡x from 0 to π (area 2), then from 0 to 2π: the result is 0 because the area below the axis cancels the area above it.

Formulas and methods

∫abf(x) dx=F(b)−F(a),F′(x)=f(x)

Adaptive Simpson's rule approximates f by parabolas on small sub-intervals,

∫x0x2f(x) dx≈h3[f(x0)+4f(x1)+f(x2)],

and keeps halving any sub-interval whose estimate is not yet accurate, until the overall error is about 10−11.

Worked example

∫03(x2+1) dx

Step 1 — Antiderivative

F(x)=x33+x

Step 2 — Evaluate

F(3)−F(0)=(9+3)−0=12

Assumptions, domain and rounding

  • f must be defined and finite everywhere on [a,b]. Improper integrals (an infinite limit, or a vertical asymptote inside the interval, as with 1x on [−1,1]) are rejected.
  • Limits may be expressions such as pi/2 or e.
  • Polynomials with rational limits give exact fractions. Other exact-method results and all numerical results are decimals; numerical values are shown to 9 decimal places.
